newsitem.title: GERMANY: Adidas CEO says erred on U.S. basketball shoe campaign.
newsitem.headline: Adidas CEO says erred on U.S. basketball shoe campaign.

text.p: The chief executive of Adidas AG, which reported higher profits on strong North American sales, said Tuesday he believed the company had erred in its efforts to break into the basketball shoe market in the United States.

"If I had to do it again, maybe I would have approached the stars and then developed the product," Chief Executive Robert Louis-Dreyfus said in an interview. "We made a mistake" in doing the reverse."

Louis-Dreyfus, a former top executive at advertising firm Saatchi & Saatchi, inherited the strategy -- which was to create products and then seek endorsements -- when he took control of the then-troubled sports brand in December 1991.

Adidas, which Tuesday reported 44 percent growth in North American sales, announced in August that it was again seeking to make inroads in the massive U.S. basketball shoe market against Nike Inc. and Reebok International Ltd with the launch of a new high-tech shoe.
The shoe, called the Equipment Top Ten 2000, was launched with a $20 million campaign developed by Leagas Delaney.
The shoe is endorsed by Kobe Bryant, a first-round draft pick last year in the National Basketball Association who jumped to the NBA straight from high school.
"It was absolutely the right thing to do but maybe we should have signed a Kobe Bryant two years ago," Louis-Dreyfus said about signing Bryant to an endorsement contract.
Although sales of the new shoe -- one of the company's "Feet You Wear" shoes, which are designed to mirror the foot -- were very strong, he said overall basketball shoe sales were weak.
"We have had some bad categories in the States and basketball is not doing well," he said. "With basketball, we will be down against last year's levels."
Adidas is predicting growth in the number of shoes sold and sees 20 percent growth in the number of textile pieces sold in North America.
"It's not as quick as I would like but it is still doing well," he said of North American sales, while also repeating his goal for $1.5 billion in sales by 2000.

The sports brand, known for its three-stripe logo, has seen its overall U.S. sales surge in recent years, moving up to No. 3 last year behind Nike and Reebok with sales of $680 million. It was No. 8 three years ago.

Louis-Dreyfus also said Adidas would follow its "guerrilla campaign" strategy of targeting specific areas of North America with specialised advertising to attract customers instead of the broad-market campaigns used by its rivals.
"I think we are a year and a half away from dropping the guerrilla tactics," he said.
"If you look at the States, where you have big stores, we are only in 50 percent of their stores. To go with a full blown attack, we need to be in 70 to 80 percent."
Adidas said its third-quarter profits rose 17 percent to 150 million marks ($100.4 million). Sales rose 35 percent to 1.47 billion marks ($983.6 million), paced by a 44 percent gain in North America.
On a nine-month basis, Adidas' net income rose 29 percent to 324 million marks ($216.8 million) while sales surged 31 percent to 3.71 billion marks ($2.5 billion).
Adidas said its apparel sales surged 45.5 percent during the quarter while footwear sales rose 24.2 percent.
Europe was still the engine behind revenues, with sales reaching 1.01 billion marks ($674.9 million) and topping the one billion mark ($668.2 million) level for the first time in company history.
Sales in North America grew by an above-average 44 percent to 314 million marks ($209.8 million) from 218 million marks ($145.7 million), Adidas said.
